[p. 428]

**Surat Saba'**

Its central theme is that the Hereafter, which he referred to at the end of the previous surah, when he mentioned punishment and forgiveness after informing us that people ask about it, is certain to occur without any doubt. This is because of the wisdom in it and his power over it, while abandoning it would lack wisdom and would portray injustice. The story of Saba', after which the surah is named, has a great connection to this purpose, as its explanation will show. For this reason, the surah is named after it. "In the name of Allah" (Bismillah) indicates that his power is comprehensive enough to establish reckoning. "The Most Merciful" (al-Rahman) indicates that his general mercy includes the arrangement of reward and punishment. "The Especially Merciful" (al-Rahim) indicates that he bestows upon the people of His honor, through their obedience to Him, that no punishment or reproach will reach them.

When the surah of al-Ahzab was concluded with the statement that He, glory be to Him, offered the trust (amanah), and its bearing, which is all the benefits in existence, to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they refused to bear it out of fear, while humankind, which includes both humans and jinn, bore it, and that the result of the offering, the fulfilling and the bearing is punishment and reward, it becomes known that all of it belongs to Him and is within His dominion. They fear His greatness and are apprehensive of the subjugation of His might, and His majesty overpowers all. He is the complete Owner of ownership and the King who is obeyed, who disposes of everything without any resistance. He concluded that with the two attributes of forgiveness and mercy. He pointed to all of this by beginning this surah with His saying: ﴿Praise (al-hamd)﴾, which means the encompassing of all attributes of perfection, in creation and command, absolutely, in the first life and the next and in other matters that can exist and that His knowledge, glory be to Him, encompasses. ﴿belongs to Allah﴾, Possessor of majesty and beauty.

Since this was the intended meaning, He described Himself with what conveys it. He said, drawing attention first to the blessing of origination and perpetuation: ﴿to Whom belongs﴾, meaning alone, in ownership and dominion, even if you attribute ownership and dominion to others in an apparent sense, ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾, meaning all of them, ﴿and whatever is on the earth﴾, meaning as you see that no one other than Him has complete disposal over any of that. It is known in many places and established in every natural disposition that He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne. Thus it follows that He owns whatever His Throne contains of the heavens and the lands and what is in them, because it is known that the Throne encompasses everything, so everything is within it, and every heaven is within the one above it, and likewise the lands. It has been established that He owns whatever is in all of it, so it follows that He owns all of it by this sound proof. This is more eloquent than if it had been expressed explicitly. Since He owns all of that, there is no blessing upon anything except from Him, so everything praises Him for the blessings He has bestowed upon it, with the tongue of speech, or if not, with the tongue of its state.

[p. 430]

Since this indicates that He owns this world and what is in it, and it is known at the end of al-Ahzab that the outcome of existence is punishment and forgiveness, and we see that most wrongdoers and hypocrites die without punishment, and most believers die without receiving what they were promised of reward, and we know with certainty that it is not permissible for a wise one to leave His servants neglected, with some transgressing against others while He does not take notice, this indicates that He has another abode in which He manifests justice and spreads generosity and grace. Therefore, He said, linking it to what the first statement implies, such as: "So to Him belongs praise in the first life," and He concealed it because it is hidden from most of creation, and He manifested what is in the Hereafter because it is manifest, as it is the abode of the unveiling of the veil. He said, drawing attention second to the blessing of return and perpetuation: ﴿And to Him belongs﴾, meaning alone, ﴿praise (al-hamd)﴾, meaning the encompassing of perfection, ﴿in the Hereafter﴾, manifestly, for everyone whom the gathering assembles, and to Him belongs everything in it. No one claims any part of it, neither apparently nor inwardly. Everything in it is manifest in praise at that time, praising Him as is befitting His majesty, for the blessings He has bestowed upon it. The least of these is the blessing of existence. Even the people of the Fire praise Him for what was made beloved to them in this world of His abundant blessings, both apparent and hidden, including sending down the Books and sending the Messengers in a manner that left no room for them to love Him in calling them to Him and turning to Him, and offering counsel in ways of gentleness, as is known to those who experienced it. They know that they were the ones who fell short, as they refused in the first life, when faith would have benefited, and they acknowledged it in the Hereafter, when the time had passed. ﴿And they will say, "We have believed in Him." But how could they reach [Him] from a place so far?﴾ [Saba' 52], and so on in the verses. Also, they praise Him in the Hereafter because they know that He does not punish any of them beyond what they deserve, although He is capable of doing so. For this reason He made the Fire into levels and arranged it into degrees. They were praising in the first life in other than the proper manner, so their praise did not benefit them, since it was built on other than a foundation. They praised in the Hereafter in the proper manner, but it did not avail them, because it is not the abode of action, and its condition was lost, which is faith in the unseen. The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device where two omitted parts complement each other): he omitted first "to Him belongs praise in the first life" because of what the second part indicates, and second "and to Him belongs everything in the Hereafter" because of what the first part indicates. It has become known from this, and from what I mentioned in al-Nahl and al-Fatihah, that praise (hamd) is sometimes considered in relation to the one who praises, and sometimes in relation to the one praised. The second is the attribution of beauty to the one praised, and the first is the praiser's description of Him with beauty. So Allah's praise, exalted is He, is His attribution to Himself of every beautiful attribute, and the praise of the praiser for Him is his describing Him with that. Thus all the created beings speak with the tongues of their states in praise of Him, whether the tongue of speech utters it or not, and He is praised before their creation. That is the meaning of my earlier statement: the encompassing of attributes of perfection. Others' praise of Him is sometimes used in its linguistic meaning, and sometimes in its conventional meaning.

[p. 432]

The verification of what the scholars said about this, in itself and in its relation to gratitude (shukr), is that praise (hamd) linguistically is the description of something with an beauty that is voluntary, out of glorification, its locus is the tongue alone, so it is specific to the outward, and its object is blessing or other things. Its locus is specific and its object is general. Gratitude (shukr), linguistically, is the reverse of this: its object is specific and its locus is general, because it is an act that indicates glorifying the benefactor on account of his bestowal. Its locus is the outward and the inward, since it encompasses the tongue, the heart and the limbs, and its object is the blessing reaching the thankful one. Among its loci is the heart, which is the most noble of all loci, because the act of the heart, though hidden, stands on its own as gratitude without any other act being added to it, unlike the other two loci, since no act of either of them is praise or gratitude in truth unless the act of the heart is joined to it.

Since the reversal of the loci and the objects is clearly indicative of the relation between praise and gratitude in their linguistic senses, it is known that between them there is a general and specific relation in both directions. Praise may follow from mere virtues, while gratitude may be specific to favours. Thus praise is distinct in this respect, and gratitude is distinct in outward action and inward belief in favours without speech. They coincide in the inner and tongue-related description of favours. The act of the heart is the belief that the one being thanked is characterized by the attributes of perfection, of majesty and beauty. The act of the tongue is the mention of what indicates that, and the act of the limbs is performing actions that indicate that.

Since this is the reality of praise and gratitude linguistically, and not conventionally, and since people's imaginations tend to think that praise is what includes the root ḥ-m-d, al-Qutb al-Razi said in his commentary on al-Matali' (Sharh al-Matali'): Praise is not an expression of the particular statement of the speaker ["al-hamdu lillah" (praise belongs to Allah)], although this statement is one instance of the reality. Likewise, the reality of gratitude is not an expression of the particular statement of the speaker ["al-shukru lillah" (thanks belongs to Allah)], nor the unrestricted statement that indicates glorifying Allah, although the second is a part of it and the first is one instance of this part. The conventional reality of praise is what indicates glorifying the benefactor on account of his being a benefactor. The conventional reality of gratitude is the servant's directing of all that Allah has bestowed upon him of faculties to what He created them for, such as directing the sight to contemplating His creations for reflection toward His exalted presence, casting the hearing toward receiving what informs of His pleasure, and abstaining from what He forbids. The mention of the attribute in the linguistic sense conveys speech, whether it is internal or verbal, so it includes Allah's praise of Himself and our praise of Him. The beautiful encompasses blessing and other noble character traits and good deeds. The non-restriction of the attribute to being in return for His blessings is a sign, because praise may occur in return for a blessing and may not. The condition of glorification conveys the agreement of the outward and the inward. If the tongue's speech is not in accordance with belief, or the actions of the limbs contradict it, it is not praise in truth, but mockery and derision. The agreement of the heart and the limbs is a condition of praise, not a component of it, so the two definitions do not overlap. The eternal attributes of Allah are not excluded by the voluntary, since from the standpoint of His power over attaching them to things, they are included, so praise is for the voluntary attribute. Likewise, when the brave man is praised for his bravery and for the power to attach the attribute to what realizes it, bravery is only special, and there is no one praised for it. It has become known from this that when there is choice in the effects, praise is due for it, otherwise not. So the description of a pearl with the purity of its substance and the delight of its appearance is not called praise but commendation (madh). The description of bravery, due to choice in manifesting its effects, is called praise. Thus praise is specific to the voluntary agent, unlike commendation. It has also become known that the specific statement, "al-hamdu lillah," is not praise because of its specificity, but because it indicates the attribute of perfection and manifests it. Therefore every other description indicating that shares in the naming. For this reason some verifying Sufis said: The reality of praise is the manifestation of attributes of perfection. This may be by speech, as is known, and may be by action, which is stronger, because actions, which are the effects of attributes, indicate them with a certain rational and definite indication, in which no contradiction can be imagined, unlike speech, whose indication of them is conventional, and its indicated meaning may fail to occur. Allah, exalted is He, has praised Himself with what is certain in speech and action. As for action, He spread the carpet of existence over countless possibilities and placed upon it the tables of His endless generosity. This uncovers His attributes of perfection and manifests them with definite detailed indications that are endless, since every atom of existence indicates them. Such indications cannot be conceived in the expressions of the created. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I cannot enumerate praise of You; You are as You have praised Yourself." It is necessary, for attention to what Abu al-Hasan al-Tujibi al-Maghribi al-Hirali, the teacher, said in his tafsir, that the praise formula of al-Fatihah contains, from its outward aspect, complete and perfect praise from one who sees praise pervading everything Allah originated and perfected of causes, which the whole cosmos contains. It is known that both of His Lord's hands are a blessed right hand. This is the meaning of what the encompassing knowledge manifests, through Allah's manifestation of His wisdom in a way with no denial in it from Him, nor from one who is His successor in His command. It is not among the meanings of what is between the servant and his Lord from the aspect of bestowing blessings, which is a matter the heart finds as knowledge, not a matter that accords with the soul's desire. Whoever does not perfect this knowledge, following upon a trace of its knowledge, finding the blessing of its recitation, [has not understood]. End.

Ami al-qawl (speech), He, glory be to Him, knew that the tongue of circumstance signals only by a hidden allusion, which none grasps except the discerning few, even though after investigation it becomes clear. So He sent down to us a Book that expresses the intended meaning plainly. In it He praised Himself and explained the attributes of His perfection (p-436) with an eloquence that the most capable cannot match. Then He made the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Book a decisive proof of His perfection and of all His majesty and beauty.

From these definitions it is known that between the linguistic hamd (praise) and the linguistic shukr (gratitude) there is a general-and-specific relation from one aspect. This is because hamd may follow from excellences ([namely, the attributes]) that are beautiful and whose effect and benefit do not pass beyond the one praised, such as courage. Shukr is specific to bounties (fawa'il), which are blessings, and these are the attributes and qualities that transfer, from which a benefit reaches others than the one praised, such as kindness, gifts and largesse, as has passed.

Between the customary (, 'urfi) hamd and shukr there is a general-and-specific relation that is absolute. Hamd is absolutely more general, because the blessings reaching the one who praises and others than him are common, whereas shukr is restricted to what reaches the one who gives thanks. This is because the benefactor mentioned in the definition is unrestricted; it is not specified as being a benefactor to the one who praises or to someone else. So it encompasses both. This is contrary to shukr, in which a specific benefactor is stipulated, namely Allah, Exalted is He, and blessings reaching the one who gives thanks from Him.

There is a second aspect to the absolute generality of this hamd and the absolute specificity of this shukr: an act of the heart or the tongue, for example, may be hamd and not shukr at all, since the inclusion of the instruments is stipulated in shukr.

A third aspect is that shukr in this sense does not relate to anyone other than Him, Exalted is He, unlike hamd. (p-437) As for what is said, namely that the relation between the two customary terms is a general-and-specific relation that is absolute only in terms of existence and not in terms of predication (haml), which is our subject, because the praise by directing the heart, for example, toward what it was created for, is a part of directing the whole, and it is not predicated of it since it is distinguished in existence from its other parts; but in predication, the predicate is not distinguished from the subject in external existence. So this is an error arising from confusing a thing with what it applies to. For what is not predicated of that directing is what hamd applies to, namely the directing of the heart alone and not its stated concept, which is an act indicating the magnification of the benefactor by reason of his being a benefactor. This concept is predicated of the directing of the whole.

As for what is said, that the directing of the whole consists of multiple acts and therefore cannot truly be described as one act, its answer is that it is one act whose object is multiple, so this does not contradict its description as one. Thus one says: "one act proceeded from Zayd, namely honouring all the people," for example. The verification of this is that a compound may be described as one in the true sense, like one body, or in the conventional sense, like one army. The application of "all" is of the second kind, as no one of sound judgment doubts. The relation between the linguistic and customary senses of hamd is a general-and-specific relation from one aspect, because customary hamd is linguistic shukr, and the explanation of this has passed for both.

Between customary shukr (p-438) and linguistic shukr there is an absolute general relation, because linguistic shukr covers blessing toward another, whereas customary shukr does not; so the former is more general and the latter is absolutely more specific. Likewise between customary shukr and linguistic hamd, because the former is restricted to a blessing upon the one who gives thanks, whether by tongue or not, while the latter, even if restricted to the tongue, requires agreement of the limbs and the heart so that it is in the manner of veneration, and it may not be in return for a blessing. So it is absolutely more general, and therefore every customary shukr is linguistic hamd, but not conversely. This holds in terms of existence.

Likewise between customary hamd and linguistic shukr there is also an absolute general relation, if the blessing in the linguistic sense is restricted to its reaching the one who gives thanks, as has passed. If it is not restricted, the two are identical. As for unrestricted shukr, it is, by analogy with what has passed, the magnification of the benefactor by directing his blessing toward what pleases him. It is not hidden that if the very act of hamd and shukr is itself among the blessings, then no one can perform them in full and complete form, since that would require an infinite regress of acts. This verification is transmitted from Imam al-Haramayn and Imam al-Razi. This is the substance of what is in Sharh al-Matali' by Qutb al-Razi and its gloss by al-Sharif al-Jurjani, with additions. The soundness of what I have stated in the explanation of hamd, both with regard to the one who praises and with regard to the one praised, is now known. When you gather the scattered points stated earlier in Surat al-Nahl (p-439) and al-Fatiha and elsewhere, namely that the root revolves around encompassing, it becomes known that with regard to the one who praises, the description of the one praised is encompassing of the attributes of perfection; and with regard to the one praised, his being characterized by encompassing the attributes of perfection. For the description must be stipulated to correspond, otherwise it is mere eulogy (madh) and not hamd, as Shams al-Din Ahmad ibn Khalil al-Khoyyi, the scholar and Qadi of Damascus, verified in his book Aqalim al-Ta'alim.

Since it has been established that wisdom (hikmah, the knowledge of things in their correct form, connected with acting in accordance with it) is not complete except by bringing about the Hereafter, He said: ﴿And He is the All-Wise﴾, meaning, whose wisdom has reached the final point beyond which there is no more.

Since wisdom cannot be attained except through the subtle, pure and essential knowledge, which is expertise (khibrah), He said: ﴿the All-Aware﴾, meaning, the one of thorough awareness, which is knowledge of the outward and inward of affairs, in state and in outcome. So it is not permissible in reason that He, who is characterized by these two attributes, as is observed in the perfection of His acts and the precision of everything, and as we have heard from His words, should create creation in vain without a return for the abode of recompense. And it has passed in al-Fatiha and elsewhere, from the scholar Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani, that he said: "Opening with praise is a reference to the four fundamental blessings: the first origination, the second origination, the first preservation, and the second preservation. Because al-Fatiha is the Mother of the Book, all of them are indicated in it (p-440). Then in every surah that begins after it with praise, one blessing from among them is indicated in order. In al-An'am, the first origination is indicated, which is obvious. In al-Kahf, the first preservation is indicated, because the arrangement of the first preservation and benefit from origination is not possible except through the Book and the Messenger. In this surah, the second origination is indicated, because the discourse proceeds to establish resurrection and to refute those who deny the Hour, where He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And those who disbelieved said: The Hour will not come to us. Say: Yes, by my Lord﴾ [Saba': 3]." End of quote. It has been known from what I have established that from its very beginning it points to this by way of proof.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: It was opened with "Praise be to Allah" because it follows what Surat al-Ahzab contains of great favours and magnificent bounties, as I have clarified just now, meaning at the end of his discussion of Surat al-Ahzab. So it was a fitting occasion for praise for what He bestowed upon His believing servants and gave them. Thus He, exalted, said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, in ownership and origination. This indicates the suppression of one who, cut off from understanding His disposal of His servants by what preceded and by His distinguishing them according to what He wills, hesitates, as if it were said: since they are His property and slaves, He should not hesitate in His action toward them, whatever He does of facilitation toward the best (p-441) or for other reasons, which He wills for them, seeking to understand its cause and to inquire into its reason. Rather, He does with them what He wills and intends, without restraint or prevention. ﴿And He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware﴾: the wisdom behind that, which is hidden from you.

His words ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾ indicate that He will make His believing servants know, from among the requirements of His praise, what He grants them or multiplies for them of recompense or great reward in the Hereafter, beyond what their minds reached in this world and what their thoughts could encompass: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17]. Then He, glory be to Him, followed what preceded of His praise, as He deserves, by displaying the evidences of His wisdom and knowledge. He said, exalted is He: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends into it﴾ [Saba': 2] up to His words ﴿And He is the Most Merciful, the Forgiving﴾ [Saba': 2]. So by His mercy and forgiveness He bestowed upon His believing servants what He singled them out with and gave them. Thus to Him belongs the praise that is due to Him. Then He followed this with mention of His forbearance toward lies and disbelief, despite their great audacity, so that the vastness of His mercy and forgiveness might become manifest. He said, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved said: The Hour will not come to us﴾ [Saba': 3] up to His words: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for every returning servant﴾ [Saba': 9]. That is, in His, glory be to Him, forbearance toward these people, after their arrogance and their mockery in their saying ﴿The Hour will not come to us﴾ [Saba': 3], and in their saying: ﴿Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you when you are completely dispersed that you will be in a new creation?﴾ [Saba': 7], and their turning away from taking heed of what is before them of heaven and earth, and their security from Him seizing them from any direction, and in His forbearance toward them and His abundant provision for them despite their great transgression, there are signs for whoever turns back and takes heed. Then He spread out for His believing servants, from the mention of the signs and His blessings and His disposal of His creatures, what makes clear the manifestation of His dominion and His sovereignty, and points to the magnitude of His kingdom, as He made known in His words, glory be to Him: [﴿Praise be to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, then He, glory be to Him, said]: ﴿And We had certainly given David bounty from Us. O mountains, echo the praise with him, and the birds. And We made iron pliable for him﴾ [Saba': 10]. Then He said: ﴿And to Solomon the wind﴾ [Saba': 12] up to His words: ﴿Work, O family of David, in gratitude﴾ [Saba': 13]. Then He followed this with mention of the condition of one who did not give thanks, so He mentioned the story of Saba' to its end. Then He, exalted, rebuked those who worshipped others besides Him after the matter had become clear and explained. He said: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claimed besides Allah﴾ [Saba': 22], up to His description of their state in the Hereafter and the exchange between their arrogant ones and their weak ones, and between their weak ones and their arrogant ones: ﴿And they concealed their regret when they saw the punishment﴾ [Saba': 33]. Then the verses were joined together, proceeding according to what preceded from the beginning of the surah to its end. End of quote.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 34, verse 2:

When he concluded with the attribute of reporting, he followed it with what indicates it, saying: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾, meaning this kind of thing, of waters, wealth and the dead. He mentioned this first because a thing first disappears into the dust and is then watered and emerges. ﴿And what comes out of it﴾, of waters, minerals and plants. ﴿And what descends from the sky﴾, meaning this kind of thing: heat, cold, water, angels and other things. ﴿And what ascends﴾. Since the heavens are dense bodies arranged in layers, he did not use the particle of limit (ḥarf al-ghāyah, the particle denoting an endpoint), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fāṭir: 10]. Instead he said: ﴿into it﴾, meaning of deeds, angels, and everything that rises from the earth in the direction of height. You see that He distinguishes each thing from its like, so He distinguishes what has the capacity to generate plants from water and earth on the earth from the rest of the water and earth of its various kinds, distinguishing some of it from others, and among minerals gold, silver, iron, copper, lead and so on. Yet all of this is mixed with the al-zābb. How, then, could it be considered remote for Him to revive the dead, given the difficulty of distinguishing the dust of each dead person after dispersal and mixing with other dust?

Since the outcome of what has preceded is that He is the Lord of everything, and since lordship cannot be properly ordered except through gentleness and reform, and since an ignorant person might suppose that He does not know the deeds of creatures, for if He knew them He would not have allowed them to stand, He informed them that His mercy precedes His wrath. For this reason he put the attribute of mercy first. Also, since this occurs within a context of praise, it was fitting to put before the attribute that relates to perfection the attribute that negates deficiency. So he said: ﴿And He﴾, meaning, while the case is that He alone, together with the abundance of His blessings which sustain bodies, ﴿is the Most Merciful﴾, meaning the Bestower of what the Divinity (al-Ilāhiyyah) is pleased with, namely the sending down of books and the sending of messengers to establish religions. ﴿The Most Forgiving﴾, meaning the Eraser of sins. As for whoever follows what was sent down of that as the messengers conveyed it, there is erasure of both its substance and its trace, so that He does not punish them for what has passed and does not reproach them. As for others, expiation comes through various kinds of trials, or through delay until the Day of Gathering.

When His wisdom was established by what we witness of firm deeds and sound sayings, His knowledge was thereby established too, since wisdom is not possible without knowledge. The Lord, the Merciful, the All-Knowing, does not attain the perfection of His lordship except through manifest sovereignty and overpowering dominion that is free of any admixture. Thus the Resurrection was established, for it is the place of wisdom and the locus where justice becomes manifest. The result of this is: "Allah brings the Hour, since its proofs have been established, as you see." Then He joined to it His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾, meaning they concealed what their intellects pointed to of its manifest proofs: ﴿The Hour will not come upon us﴾. Their report about it is false.

Since the proofs already presented leave no room for doubt, He commanded him to answer them by rejecting their statement, emphasizing with an oath that He had not left him without a clear proof. So He said: ﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord﴾, that is, the One who has been good to me by the blessings He has bestowed upon me along with you, by the prophethood He has singled me out with and my sending to you, and by other matters that none can count except Him, glorified is He. He is too generous to leave you without gathering you, so that He may take retribution on my behalf and gladden my eye by recompensing you for your harm to me and to those who follow me. No master ever accepts that some of his disobedient servants should oppress others and leave them neglected without discipline. How much more so when the one oppressed is obedient to Him and the oppressor is disobedient to Him! No rational person accepts this, so how could a judge accept it, and how could the Most Just of judges accept it? ﴿Surely it will come upon you﴾, that is, (p. 445) the Hour, so that wisdom with justice and grace, and the other wonders of judgment and decision, may be fully manifest in it.

Since a judge does not neglect his subjects unless they are absent from his knowledge, and does not neglect any of their affairs unless that thing is absent from him, and since the Hour belongs to the unseen realm, and since what preceded regarding the establishment of knowledge might be restricted by a contrarian to the realm of the witnessed, He described His Most Holy Self, glorified is He, in a way that shows there is no difference before Him between the unseen, of which the Hour is part, and the witnessed. Rather, all of it is witnessed before Him. For the sake of this meaning, the unseen is mentioned first when the two are combined in mention. He said, declaring the greatness of the One sworn by, so as to establish the truth of what is sworn to, since an oath stands in place of invoking testimony for a matter. The more exalted, more evident in virtue, and higher in rank the one invoked as witness, the stronger and more emphatic the testimony, and the firmer and more established what is attested. He describes Him, according to the reading of the majority and as a resumptive (isti'naf, a new sentence that resumes the discourse), which is more eloquent according to the reading of the people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir, and Ruways from Ya'qub, in the nominative: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾. The reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i is ʿAllām, in the intensive form (mubalagha, emphatic intensification), as is more fitting to the context.

Since we, because of the shortcoming of our knowledge, are restricted to what is in this world, while the discussion is about it, (p. 446) He stated the intended meaning explicitly in the most complete manner: ﴿Not escaping Him﴾, that is, not hidden or remote, with a strong absence according to the reading of the majority with a ḍamma, nor a weak one according to the reading of al-Kisa'i with a kasra. ﴿Is an atom's weight﴾, that is, of any essence or meaning. The dharra (atom, tiny ant) is a very small red ant that became a proverb for the least of the least, so it is a kinaya (metonymy) for it. Since this surah is concerned with praise, which is perfection, and since the most fitting direction of loftiness for it is praise, and since the matter of the Hour and its beginning is from it, He began with it.

Since He had made clear His knowledge of the affairs of the heavens, and since what was meant by them is the genus, He gathered them here to make that intent explicit, saying: ﴿in the heavens﴾, and He emphasized the negation by repeating ﴿nor﴾, saying: ﴿nor on the earth﴾. Since we are restricted by the Book, He began the report with what dazzles the intellect: that everything is inscribed before it comes into being and then occurs in accordance with what was inscribed. When this is unveiled to the angels, they increase in faith, glorification, praise, and sanctification. He said, according to all the reciters, joining it as a sentence to what precedes, not to "atom's weight," because the exception prevents that: ﴿Nor smaller than that﴾, that is, there is nothing smaller than that, meaning the atom's weight, ﴿nor greater﴾, that is, than the atom's weight, and whatever is above it, ﴿but it is in a Book﴾. Our reporting of it is because of our customary practice of restricting knowledge to a book. As for Him, glorified is He, He has no need of that.

Since a person may write something and then forget it and forget where it is, so that he cannot retrieve it, He reported that His Book is not like that. Rather, whoever wants to be informed of anything in it finds it immediately, because it reveals nothing except that it is in utmost clarity. He said: ﴿clear﴾. It is also permissible, and perhaps better, when you consider this together with the verse of Yunus, that ﴿atom's weight﴾ be conjoined to it and that the exception be disjunctive (munqati', an exception that does not fall under the same category), while still operating as an exception in that it stands between two opposites. The meaning is that nothing of that is absent from Him or remote from Him, but it is preserved in the most perfect preservation in a Book which, when anything is sought from it to be revealed, is in the utmost clarity. Perhaps He expressed it with the particle of the connected exception to indicate that if there is any absence, it is of this kind, which is the furthest thing from absence. (p. 447)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 34, verse 4:

Then he explained the cause of all that as evidence for the truthfulness of the oath, by means of the wisdom with which the surahs (al-Ahzab) were concluded, namely the wisdom of offering the Trust (amanah), which no person of intellect doubts, even slightly, in its soundness; and that it is not permissible in wisdom for Him to do otherwise. So He said: ﴿That He may reward those who have believed﴾, meaning: indeed He did not create the universes except for the sake of mankind, so it is not permissible that He leave him without recompense. ﴿And done righteous deeds﴾, meaning: as a confirmation of their faith.

When the listener turned to knowing their reward, He presented it, magnifying its station, as an answer to the question, pointing to it with that which indicates the loftiness of its rank through the loftiness of the rank of its people: ﴿Those﴾ (p-448) meaning, those of high rank, ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾, meaning for their slips or lapses, because man, being founded on deficiency, cannot esteem the Mighty Sovereign as He deserves. ﴿And a noble provision﴾, meaning: one that is magnificent, mighty, lasting, delicious, beneficial, and pleasant, with no turbidity in it in any respect.

When the proofs of the Hour had become so clear that nothing remained preventing belief in them except obstinacy, and the context was a threat to those who denied it, He said, using the past tense: ﴿And those who strove﴾, i.e., [did] the act of one who strives, ﴿against Our signs﴾ [i.e., given their great magnitude], ﴿seeking to frustrate [them]﴾, i.e., exerting themselves in the intent to render them powerless by their failure to come to pass despite Our causing them to be carried out. Such is also the meaning of the reading with the mufa'ala form (mu'ajizin). And since their sin was great, He indicated it with a fresh beginning and said: ﴿Those﴾ [i.e., the distant, the hateful, the contemptible, who are too far beneath to attain their aim through their frustrating efforts], ﴿for them is a punishment﴾, and what a punishment ﴿of a rijz﴾, i.e., a thing wholly consisting of turmoil, which therefore brings about great distress and agitation, so it is the worst of punishments, ﴿painful﴾, i.e., of intense pain. The majority read it in the genitive as an adjective of rijz, while Ibn Kathir and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read it in the nominative as an adjective of 'adhab.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 34, verse 6:

When He had censured the disbelievers and marvelled at them for their denial of the Hour, in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "The Hour will not come upon us."﴾ [Saba': 3], [and] had established the proof of its coming, and made clear that nothing other than it is permissible in wisdom, so that justice and grace might be realised in the recompense of the people of evil and the people of grace, He followed this with praise of the believers, describing them as possessors of knowledge, to inform that what caused the disbelievers to deny was ignorance. He said: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾, expressing it by sight and in the present tense, indicating [that in their practice they are not doubters, but are rather like witnesses to everything the Messenger ﷺ informed them of, and by the present tense] the continual renewal of their practice, ascending in ranks constantly, in contrast to the coarseness of those disbelievers in their steadfastness upon falsehood, which the past tense pointed to. He also indicated that their knowledge is ladunni (bestowed directly from God, without acquisition) by His saying: ﴿who have been given knowledge﴾, meaning God cast it into their hearts, so they became witnesses to its contents; even if the veil were lifted, they would gain no more certainty. This applies whether they were among the Arabs who embraced Islam or among the People of the Book. ﴿that which has been sent down to you﴾, meaning all of it, concerning the matter of the Hour and other things, ﴿from your Lord﴾, meaning the One who bestowed favour upon you by sending it down. [The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) was brought to magnify the matter and to make explicit that what follows is the second object of "ūtū" (were given), so He said]: ﴿it is the truth﴾, meaning none other than it of speech. ﴿And guides﴾, meaning [renews over the course of time the guidance of] whoever follows it ﴿to the path﴾, meaning a clear, broad way.

Since this surah is Meccan, and the disbelievers in it were dominant while the believers were few and fearful, and the Arabs would reproach them for opposing their people and the religion of their forefathers, and other such superstitions whose essence is establishing a supposed truth by reference to men, He said: ﴿the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾, meaning He whose path—which is Islam—whoever follows it, his Lord makes him mighty and praised, so that everything praises him, even if all creation conspires against him. For He, glorified be He, will surely manifest Himself to separate His servants, with wretchedness and happiness according to the measure of their readiness.

When Allah, glory be to Him, marvelled at the disbelievers' saying ﴿The Hour will not come upon us﴾ [Saba': 3], which contains their denial, and concluded by affirming those given knowledge, indicating that the cause of the disbelievers' denial is ignorance, whose cause is arrogance, He marvelled at them with a second marvelling, more intense than the first, because they openly denied in a strange manner. So He said: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, meaning those who had ascertained his matter (ﷺ), agreed in opposing him, and persisted obstinately, saying to whoever refutes them from among those who do not know the reality of his situation, both marvelling at it and trying to deter people: ﴿Shall we direct you﴾, meaning, O you who believe there is no gathering (ḥashr, the assembly of creatures for judgment). When they put their speech in the form of strange and laughable things, they did not mention his name, although it is the most famous of names. Instead they said: ﴿to a man﴾, meaning he is not a child or a woman, so that you could excuse him, ﴿who will inform you﴾, meaning who will tell you (p-451) [whenever you wish], with a report that has no greater magnitude than what it contains of wonder that lies outside what we can comprehend [renewing that whenever the one asking him wishes].

Since their intention was to mention what, in their view, indicates the improbability of resurrection (al-ba'th), they placed the complement first and said: ﴿When﴾ [meaning, that is, when] ﴿you are torn apart﴾, meaning you are cut up and scattered after your death by everything whose nature it is to tear apart, such as dust, winds, the passage of long time and the like, with a great tearing, to the point that you become dust. This is the meaning of ﴿every tearing﴾, meaning every kind of tearing, so that no part of your bodies remains together with another part. Rather, all of it becomes such that its dust cannot be distinguished from the dust of the earth, and the floods carry it off in every direction, so that, mixed with the earth's dust and confused with it, it becomes scattered, each part far from the others. The complement of ﴿will inform you﴾ was broken off (i.e. the clause was split) because of the lam, and so he said: ﴿Indeed you are in﴾, meaning that you will stand again as you were before death, a standing about which there is no doubt, and the report of it deserves the utmost emphasis, ﴿a new creation﴾. This is the governing element of the temporal ʿidhā (إذا, "when").

Al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar, on Surah 34, verse 8:

When they repelled him from this astonishing report about the one who bears it to him, they confused the matter by dividing their speech about it into a questioning that hovered between mocking, as an expression of wonder, and denial. So they said, answering one who asked about the cause of his report (with the elision of the hamzat al-wasl, since there is no ambiguity here, unlike when it accompanies the definite article, for then its vowel would make it ambiguous with the report): ﴿Has he invented against God﴾, that is, deliberately fabricated, ﴿against God﴾ [that is] the One than whom there is nothing greater, ﴿a lie﴾ by reporting contrary to what is the case [while he is sane, so that intention is valid from him]. Since deliberate fabrication requires reason, they said: ﴿Or is there madness in him?﴾, that is, insanity, so that he speaks falsehood, which is that which has no reality, without deliberate intent, [since he is not one of the people of intention. So the verse is of the type of ihtibak (complementary omission): mention of "fabrication" first indicates its opposite second, and mention of "madness" second indicates the mention of its opposite first].

Since the answer was: there is none of that in him, He followed it, informing about some of those who disbelieved in a way that necessitates deterring the others, with His saying: ﴿Nay, those who do not believe﴾, that is, [do not] renew faith, because they have been sealed upon disbelief, ﴿in the Hereafter﴾, that is, the final creation, the one to which the first creation is the most indicative proof. Since this statement is caused by their misguidance, and their misguidance is a cause of their punishment, He placed the punishment first, because it is the destination, and so that whoever God wills to have faith is deterred. He said: ﴿in the punishment﴾, that is, in this world by attempting to nullify what God wills to complete, and in the Hereafter because of the disobedience in it. He then followed it with its cause, saying: ﴿and the error﴾, that is, from what necessarily follows of the obligation of His oneness and the comprehensiveness of His power, because of the fact that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth.

Since their statement was far from the truth, in that they described the most guided of people as misguided, and since error becomes far-reaching in proportion to the distance of its possessor from the right path and his plunging into vast, rugged deserts, He said, describing it with the description of one who is astray: ﴿far-off﴾. The description thus made clear that it is impossible to be detached from it. It is known that among those who disbelieved there is a group who were not sealed upon disbelief, who had chosen a near error from which they could be detached, and they are those among them who believed afterward. This is among the wondrous expressions, in that he used the apparent noun, which conveyed this division, in place of the pronoun, which should have been: "Nay, they are in such-and-such."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 34, verse 9:

When they denied the Hour, being certain that whoever has been torn to shreds in every piece cannot be restored, they were ignorant that Allah, exalted is He, does not say this. So they attributed the truthful one (ﷺ) in his report of this to one of two matters: deliberately lying or madness. He, glorified is He, began to show His truthfulness in all that he reported, so He started by establishing His power over that, grounding it in their misguidance due to their heedlessness of contemplating the signs. The meaning was: they went astray and so did not see. He pointed this out, rebuking them, threatening them, and establishing it for those among the listeners who possess intellects, with His saying: ﴿Have they not looked﴾. He alerted [us] that they are in a place far from beneficial sight by using the particle of limit (ilā, "to"), so He said: ﴿at what is before them﴾, that is, in front of them, ﴿and what is behind them﴾. This is an indication of all directions from each of the two horizons (al-khāfiqān), and that the two have encompassed them just as they encompass others. Since there was no need for the plural, He used the singular and said: ﴿of the heaven and the earth﴾, that is, those whom we made the opening of the surah, that everything in them belongs to us.

Since denial is fitting for the station of greatness, the meaning being: We act upon them and within them as We will, He expressed it with His saying: ﴿If We will﴾, by what belongs to us of greatness. According to the reading of the majority, ﴿We cause to sink﴾, that is, to swallow up, ﴿with them﴾ [Al-Kisa'i assimilated (the two letters), to indicate that He, glorified is He, may do that in less than the blink of an eye, such that it is perceived by most people, and He may do it in a manifest way, which is more common, which is what the clear reading of the majority indicates] ﴿the earth﴾, that is, as We did to Qarun and his people. For the effect of some of Our actions upon it is not more deserving than others. ﴿Or We cause to fall upon them fragments﴾ (kisafan), with the sin vowelled with a fatha according to the reading of Hafs and with a sukun according to the reading of others, that is, pieces, ﴿from the sky﴾ likewise [so that the impact is severe, since the target is far from the clouds and the like], because it is known that We created them, and whoever brings something into being is able to do this, and this is what He intended by it. Whoever makes the context third person, namely Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, returns the pronoun to the Greatest Name, which He made the opening of the surah.

Since this is an evident matter, it produced His saying, emphasizing what they have of denial of resurrection: ﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, [in] Our power over whatever We will of each of them and in contemplation of the varieties of their transformations, ﴿is surely a sign﴾, that is, a clear indication that We deal with whoever We will in them with justice, with whatever punishment We wish, and with whoever We will with grace, with whatever reward We wish. This indicates that We are capable of everything We will of causing death and giving life and other things. We have caused Qarun and his household to sink, and the people of Lot and their followers, and We caused to fall from the sky upon the companions of the thicket on the day of the cloud pieces of fire, and upon the people of Lot stones, and We destroyed them all by that. Since signs do not benefit one who has been sealed in obstinacy, the Exalted said: ﴿For every servant﴾, that is, one who is certain that he is a nourished, weak one subjugated to what is intended of him, ﴿who turns back (munib)﴾, that is, one in whom there is the capacity to return from what the proof has made clear he erred in.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on Surah 34, verse 10:

When He (glorified is He) indicated, through this discourse that demonstrates the absolute authority of His command, that He sometimes does justice and sometimes bestows grace, and since grace attracts those of lofty aspirations and noble souls more, He began with it regarding one of the leaders of those who turn penitently (to God), in a manner that points to the resurrection through the perfect exercise of control over the two worlds (the heavens and the earth) and what is in them, through matters witnessed by some of His servants, sometimes by sight and sometimes by hearing. As for the People of the Book, this is clear. As for the Arabs, (it is evident) from their being enabled to question them about it, for they used to ask them about him (ﷺ). Abu Hayyan said: Some of that appeared in their reports and their poetry spoke of it. So He, exalted is He, said, swearing an oath to alert (the listener) that their denial of the resurrection is a denial of what he reports of the miracles, and linking it to what is implied as its supposition: "Indeed We bestowed upon this man, whom you attributed to lying or madness, a grace from Us, by these reports indicated by the inimitable Qur'an. How far (is the distance) between [him and] what you attributed to him!" ﴿And indeed﴾ [i.e.] by Our might and by what is established for Us of encompassing the attributes of perfection, by being described with praise, indeed ﴿We gave﴾, i.e. We gave a great giving, indicating the utmost capability by what We possess of greatness, ﴿to Dawud﴾.

Since the one given may be an intermediary for the one from whom the giving comes, He clarified that the matter is nothing but from Him, so He said: ﴿from Us, a grace﴾. It indicates that the tanwin (indefinite ending) is for glorification, and that the bringing into being of anything does not depend on anything other than His will, by His saying (the word "Be"). He made the mountains like rational beings who hasten to comply with His commands, as an alert to the completeness of His power and the wondrous nature of His control over all things, as an answer to one who seems to have said: "What is that grace?" Replacing (a clause) for "We gave" (*mubdilan min "ataynā"*): ﴿O﴾, i.e. We said to the hardest of the earth: O ﴿mountains, echo back﴾, i.e. repeat the glorification and the recitation of the Psalms and other remembrance of God ﴿with him﴾, i.e. whenever he glorified. This is a terrestrial sign from what is hardest of the earth, through what is the function of rational beings. For this reason He expressed it with the imperative, indicating the greatness of the power.

Since the mountains are the coarsest and heaviest of the earth, and the meaning is: We called the mountains to echo with him, so they hastened to answer Our call, because they were previously mentioned as among those who refused to bear the trust, He followed that with the lightest and most delicate of animals, so that it would be a heavenly sign, indicating that He does what He wills in the sky, for if He caused the bird to die in the atmosphere of the sky, it would fall, and there is no difference in that between one high and another high. So He said: ﴿and the birds﴾, i.e. We called them too, and they were echoing the remembrance with him. Their being joined with the mountains indicates that their remembrance is real, like the remembrance of the mountains, to repel the misconception of one who thinks it is the echo of a sound. The reading of Ya'qub with the nominative (*wa-l-ṭayru*) is a conjunction with the wording of "mountains," and the reading of others (in the accusative) is a conjunction with its grammatical position. Or the waw may be in the sense of "with" (*ma'a*), or by supposing a verb from the meaning of what has passed, such as "We subjected." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: He used to say to the mountains, "Glorify," and to the birds, "Respond." Then he would take up, while reciting the Psalms, explaining that with his beautiful voice, so people never saw a sight more beautiful than that, nor heard anything more pleasant than it. This is like how the pebbles glorified in the hand of the Prophet (ﷺ) and in the hands of Abu Bakr and ʿUmar (p-458) (may God be pleased with them both), and as food glorified in his noble presence while it was being eaten, and as the stone greeted him, and the threshold and the walls of the house said "Amen" to his supplication, and the trunk's yearning is well known, and as the lizard (*ḍabb*) testified for him, and the camel complained to him and prostrated before him, and similar things. And as the bird called the *ḥumra* came complaining about the one who had taken its eggs, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that they be returned to it out of mercy for it.

Since He mentioned the obedience of the densest of the earth and the most delicate of the animals that God created from it, He mentioned what He, glorified is He, created from that densest substance, which is the hardest of things, so He said: ﴿And We made the iron soft for him﴾, i.e. that which We brought forth from the mountains. We made it in his hand like wax; he works from it whatever he wills, without fire and without a hammer.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 34, verse 11:

Then he mentioned the reason for the softening of the iron, using the imperative form, to indicate that his work was for God. So He said: ﴿Make full coats of mail﴾, meaning long, wide coats of armour.

Since *al-sard* (the weaving of mail, "stitching," from the piercing of holes in leather and passing a thread through the place of the holes) involves passing the link through the next one, he likened the passing of a ring through another to a continuous thread with no end, through the places of the holes. So He said: ﴿and be measured in the weaving﴾, meaning in the *nasj* (weaving), such that each link is equal to its neighbour while being narrow, so that no arrow may pass through it. It should be arranged so that (p-459) no sword can tear it, and it is not so heavy on the wearer that it hinders his freedom of movement, his speed in shifting in the *kurr wa-farr* (charge and retreat), and his thrusting and striking, in cold and in heat. Apparently there were no rivets in its rings, since there was no need for them when the iron had been softened; otherwise there would have been no difference between his work and that of others, and the softening would have had no benefit. Someone who saw what was attributed to him reported that it had no rivets.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-sard* in the language means fitting one thing to another so that it becomes uniform, some of it following after the rest in succession. From this comes the saying "Fulan *sarada* the speech (he recounted the story smoothly)." This is like what God Most High did for the Prophet ﷺ at the Trench, when He softened for him that hard rock, and in another narration *al-Kudhana*, after the mattocks had no effect on it and the people had reached the utmost of their effort. He ﷺ struck it with a single blow, and in another narration he sprinkled water on it, and it became a heap of sand that was poured out, and it did not turn back a spade. This is the rock which Salman, may God be pleased with him, reported had broken their axes and mattocks, and they were unable to deal with it. The Prophet ﷺ struck it three blows, and with his striking he broke three pieces from it. With each blow a flash of light appeared, and with each flash he pronounced *takbir* (Allahu akbar). It lit up for the Companions, may God be pleased with them, what lay between the two lava plains of Medina, so that by day it was like a lamp in the middle of a dark house. They asked him about this, and the Prophet ﷺ informed them that one of the blows lit up for him San'a in the land of Yemen, until he saw its gates from that place, and Jibril, peace be upon him, informed him that it would be opened to his community. Another blow lit up for him the white palaces of al-Hira, which looked like dogs' fangs, and he informed them that it would be opened to them. Another blow lit up for him the red palaces of Sham, and he informed them of their conquest by them. God Most High confirmed him in all that he said.

Greater than this is the making of wood into a sword of strong spine and excellent iron, for "the sword of Abdullah ibn Jahsh, may God be pleased with him, broke on the day of Uhud, so the Messenger of God ﷺ gave him a palm-stalk, and it returned in his hand as a sword with a hilt from it, and he fought with it, and it was called *al-'Awn* (the Helper). It remained after that to be inherited until it was sold to Bagha al-Turki for two hundred dinars." Al-Kulla'i mentioned this in *al-Sira* from al-Zubayr ibn Abi Bakr, and al-Bayhaqi. "And 'Ukkasha ibn Mihsan fought on the day of Badr, and his sword broke, so he came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and he gave him a stick of firewood. When he took it and shook it, it returned in his hand as a sword, long in length, of strong spine and white iron, and he fought with it until God gave victory to the Muslims. That sword was called *al-'Awn*, and then it remained with him, witnessing battles with the Messenger of God ﷺ and after him, until he was killed in the Apostasy wars (p-461) while it was with him." And from al-Waqidi: "The sword of Salama ibn Aslam ibn al-Huraysh broke on the day of Badr, so the Messenger of God ﷺ gave him a rod that was in his hand, made of the palm-stalks of Ibn Tab, and said: 'Strike with it.' Then it was a good sword. It remained with him until he was killed on the day of the Bridge of Abu 'Ubayd."

His softening of the iron is no more remarkable than the Prophet ﷺ's joining of the hand of Mu'awwadh ibn 'Afra' when Abu Jahl cut it off on the day of Badr. He came carrying it in his other hand, and the Messenger of God ﷺ spat upon it and joined it, and it stuck and became sound like its fellow, as al-Bayhaqi and others transmitted.

When He, glory be to Him, completed what is specific to him of the honours, He followed them with what includes the pronoun, because it encompasses others. So He said: ﴿And work righteousness﴾, meaning you and those who obey you, ﴿righteousness﴾, meaning by what We have bestowed upon you of knowledge and success in obedience. Then He gave a reason for this command, by way of encouragement and warning, with His saying, emphasized, to indicate that their denial of the ability to resurrect is a denial of other attributes, and that one who is lax in works is among those who deny that He is watching over him: ﴿Indeed I am, of what you do﴾, meaning all of it, ﴿Seeing﴾, meaning observing and knowing everything apparent to Him and hidden.

[p-462] When God, glorified is He, had completed what He willed of the verses concerning Dawud, peace be upon him, and concluded them with iron, He followed him with his son Sulayman, peace be upon him, because of his shared turning to God (inabah). He began the verses about him with what relates to God's creation of iron, saying: ﴿And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind﴾, meaning, in place of the horses that he slaughtered for God, ﴿the wind﴾, that is, made subservient, according to the reading of Shu'bah. According to the reading of the majority (al-jama'ah), the sense is: We subjected it to him, in a state in which ﴿its morning [journey] was a month's [travel] and its evening [journey] was a month's [travel]﴾. That is, it carried him and went with him and with his entire army in the morning, from the early hours until midday, a distance of a month's travel. He would set out in the morning from Iliya and take his midday rest at Istakhr. ﴿And its evening [journey] was a month's [travel]﴾, meaning from midday until the end of the day, a month's journey. This is a heavenly sign indicating that just as He raised Sulayman's carpet, with what it carried of his soldiers and equipment, and then set it down, He is able to cast down whatever He wills from the sky, destroying whoever it falls upon. This is like God's subjecting the wind to the Prophet (ﷺ) at the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), when it toppled their tents, overturned their food, and struck their faces with stones and dust, while it did not pass beyond their camp, until God defeated them by it. It is also like how it carried two of his Companions, may God be pleased with them, at the Battle of Tabuk and cast them onto the two mountains of Tayy. And it carries whomever God wills of the saints (awliya') of his community, as is well known and widely reported. As for the matter of the Night Journey (al-Isra') and the Ascension (al-Mi'raj), it is of such majesty and greatness that none knows it but God. Moreover, God directed him through the signs of the sky, by withholding rain at times and sending it at others.

When He mentioned the wind, He followed it with what is also among the causes of its creation, saying: ﴿And We caused a spring of molten copper to flow for him﴾, meaning by Our majesty. ﴿Spring of copper (qitr)﴾, that is, brass (nuhas), which We melted for him until it became like a spring of water. This indicates that He (exalted is He) does in the earth whatever He wills. Had He willed, He could have made it all flow, and everyone upon it would perish; and had He willed, He could have made, instead of flowing, a sinking and an annihilation.

When He mentioned the wind and the copper, which ordinarily cannot be melted except by fire, He mentioned that whose elements are mostly fire, and which, in its lightness and its capacity for flight, is like the wind, saying: ﴿And of the jinn﴾, meaning, and We subjected to him from among the jinn, that is, those whom We hid from sight, of the devils and others, ﴿whoever works﴾. Since God had enabled him over them to the utmost degree of ability, both in their absence and their presence, He said: ﴿before him﴾. Since someone might suppose that they had independent authority over their own actions, He negated this by saying: ﴿by the leave of his Lord﴾, meaning by the empowerment of the Benefactor, who empowered him and them to do what He wills.

[p-464] When God, glorified is He, established that this was by His will, and so in reality it was by His command, He reinforced this confirmation by saying, in a clause connected to what is implied by the preceding context (as if to say: whoever obeys Our command, We reward with the Gardens of Bliss), ﴿And whoever of them swerves﴾, that is, turns aside, from the verb zaagha, yazigh and yazugh, ﴿from Our command﴾, [that is, from what We commanded him of obedience to Sulayman], meaning his command, which is from Our command, ﴿We will make him taste﴾, that is, by the majesty We possess, with which We enabled Sulayman, peace be upon him, from what We enabled him in this regard, ﴿the punishment of the Blaze﴾, that is, in this world figuratively, and in the Hereafter literally. This is like how God enabled our Prophet (ﷺ) over that 'ifrit: he seized him and throttled him, and he intended to tie him up so that the children of Madinah could play with him. But he released him out of courtesy toward his brother Sulayman, peace and blessings be upon them both, regarding what he had asked of God. As for the actions upon which the establishment of the religion depends, God made him independent of the jinn through the noble angels. He also empowered a group of his Companions, may God be pleased with them, over a number of the rebellious jinn. Among them was Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, when the Prophet (ﷺ) entrusted him with guarding the zakat of Ramadan. Among them was Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may God be pleased with him, who seized a being among them who was stealing from his dates, and said: "The jinn know that among them there is none stronger than I." Among them was Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may God be pleased with him, when the Prophet (ﷺ) appointed him over the charity of the Muslims; a devil from among them came to him stealing, and appeared to him in various forms, one of which was the form of an elephant. He restrained it, and its hands became bound to its neck, and he said to it: "O enemy of God!" It then complained to him of poverty and informed him that it was from the jinn of Nusaybin, and that they had once possessed Madinah, but when the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, he expelled them from it. It asked him to let it go on condition that it would not return. Among them was Buraydah, may God be pleased with him. Among them was Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, may God be pleased with him. Among them was Zayd ibn Thabit, may God be pleased with him. Among them was Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, and may God be pleased with them all, who wrestled with the devil and threw him down. Among them was Ammar ibn Yasir, may God be pleased with him, who fought the devil and threw him down, and Ammar struck the devil's nose with a stone and made it bleed. For this reason and others, Abu Hurayrah used to say: "Ammar is the one whom God protected from the devil, through the tongue of His Prophet (ﷺ)." Al-Bayhaqi recorded all of these in al-Dala'il, and I have mentioned the takhrij (sourcing) of most of them in my book Masa'id al-Nazar li'l-Ishraf 'ala Maqasid al-Suwar.

As for the spring of copper, it is what is contained in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have been given the keys to the treasuries of the earth, and dominion in this world and eternity therein, then Paradise. But I chose to be a prophet, a servant: I go hungry one day and am sated one day," and the hadith continues. This includes everything from the meadow of moist pearls to the spring of pure gold and what falls below that.

al-Tirmidhi narrated, and said it is hasan, from Abu Umamah, may God be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "My Lord offered me that the plain of Makkah be turned into gold for me. I said: No, O my Lord! Rather, let me be sated one day and hungry one day, or he said three days, or something like that. So when I am hungry, I humble myself before You and remember You; and when I am sated, I thank You and praise You." Al-Tabarani narrated with a hasan chain, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Zuhd and elsewhere, from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that "Israfil, peace be upon him, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with the keys to the treasuries of the earth and said: God has commanded me to offer you that I cause the mountains of Tihamah to move with you as emerald, ruby, gold and silver. If you wish, be a prophet-king; and if you wish, be a prophet-servant. Jibril, peace be upon him, gestured to him to be humble, so he said: a prophet-servant."

Ibn Hibban narrated it in his Sahih in abridged form from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him. He also has in the Sahih, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, may God be pleased with them both, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I was brought the keys of the world upon a dappled horse, on a saddle-cloth of fine silk." In al-Bukhari, in the account of the Battle of Uhud, from Uqbah ibn Amir, may God be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been given the keys to the treasuries of the earth, or the keys [of the earth]." This is what relates to the earth. And he (ﷺ) was further given, beyond that, that his Lord, glorified is He, strengthened him to act upon the treasuries of the heavens, at times by splitting the moon, at times by hurling the stars, at times by piercing the heavens, at times by withholding rain and at times by sending it, and in other ways by which God honored him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 34, verse 13:

When God, exalted is He, informed us that He subjected the jinn to him, He mentioned their condition in their work, as evidence that He, glory be to Him, disposes of the heavens and the earth and what is in them [and who is in them] as He wills. So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed﴾, that is, at whatever time He willed, ﴿of places of worship﴾, that is, lofty structures of palaces [and dwellings] and other things worthy of being made into mihrabs, or mosques. The mihrab (the niche or prayer-place) is the foremost part of every mosque, assembly, and house. Among what they made for him was the Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House in Jerusalem), its walls of wondrous, marvelous stone and white, yellow, and green marble, its pillars of pure white [clear] crystal, its ceilings and walls inlaid with gold, silver, pearls, rubies, musk, ambergris, and all kinds of perfume, and its floor laid with turquoise slabs, until it was the most splendid house on the face of the earth. ﴿And statues﴾, that is, fine images upon those structures, containing wondrous secrets, as they mentioned: they made for him two lions at the base of his throne and two eagles at its top; when he wished to ascend, the two lions spread their forelegs, and when he sat, the two eagles shaded him. Images were not forbidden.

(p-468) When he mentioned the palaces and their adornment, he mentioned the vessels of food, since they are the first thing sought after settling in a dwelling. So He said: ﴿And basins﴾, that is, dishes and bowls from which one eats, ﴿like cisterns﴾. The word is the plural of jabiyah, which is a large basin to which water is gathered, that is, in which water is collected. It is said: a single bowl would seat a thousand men.

When he mentioned the dishes in a manner that is wondrous and considered great, he mentioned what their food is cooked in, so He said: ﴿And cooking pots fixed firmly﴾, that is, firmly set in place with a great stability, such that they do not move from their trivets, because of their size, being like mountains. When he mentioned the dwellings and what follows them, he followed them with the command to work, indicating that he, peace and blessings be upon him, and whoever followed him, are not distracted by that from worship. So He said: ﴿Work, O family of David﴾, that is, and We said to them: enjoy and work. He indicated their closeness with the omission of the vocative particle, and their nobility by the expression "family" (ali), so He said: ﴿family of David﴾, that is, everything that brings one closer to God. ﴿In thankfulness﴾, that is, for the sake of giving thanks to Him, glory be to Him, which is exalting Him in return for His blessings, so that He may increase you of His bounty. [Or it is in the accusative of circumstance, meaning "thankful," or by an implied verb, "give thanks, thanks," because "work" carries in it the meaning of "give thanks," since working for the Benefactor is thanks to Him; and it is permissible for it to be governed by "work" as an object, its meaning being: We subjected the jinn to you to work for you whatever you wish, so work yourselves as thanks, by way of parallelism.] ﴿And few﴾ (p-469) that is, We said that while the state was that they are few.

Since the situation did not call for grandeur, as exaltation is more fitting in an expression of extreme thankfulness, He dropped the manifestation of it, so He said: ﴿Of My servants, the thankful﴾, that is, one whose motives for thanks are abundant in his outward and inward being, from his heart, tongue, and body, in thanking by directing all that God has bestowed upon him toward what pleases Him. He expressed it with the form fa'ul, indicating that those who engage in thanks in general are many, and the least of that is in a state of necessity.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 34, verse 14:

Since the death of one who possesses such magnificence of kingship, with his authority executed, his wide means, and his numerous armies, might seem unlikely, [the verse] points to its ease through the nearness of its time and the swiftness of its occurrence. This indicates the falsehood of the people's exalting of the jinn for [supposedly] reporting the unseen, after [the jinn] had been shown the like of this by being employed by [Solomon], through His saying ﴿fa-lamma﴾ ("so when") with the fa' [of consequence]. For this reason He returned to the manifestation of majesty and said ﴿qadayna﴾ ("We decreed"), and He confirmed the attribute of power with the particle of elevation, saying ﴿ʿalayhi﴾ ("upon him"), that is, Solomon, peace be upon him, ﴿al-mawta﴾ ("death"). ﴿Mā dallahum﴾ ("what indicated to them") means his armies and everyone in his dominion among the jinn and humans and others, from every near and far place, ﴿ʿalā mawtihi﴾ ("his death"), because We had given him an abundance of knowledge, great awe, and the power of his command, by which he was able to conceal his death from them. ﴿Illā dābbat al-arḍ﴾ ("except a creature of the earth"). He magnified it by this construction (iḍāfa), whose meaning implies that there is no creature of the earth other than it, because of the knowledge it conveys. Also, because it eats from every part of the earth, such as wood, stone, dust, and cloth and other things, it is most deserving of this name among beasts. What makes this more beautiful is that the verbal noun of its verb is ʾarḍ, with a fatḥa and with sukūn [i.e., arḍ and ʾarḍ], so it falls under tawriya (a double meaning, in which a word has a concealed second sense) so that the desire to learn its explanation is intensified. Then he explained that it is the termite (al-arada), by His saying, as a new sentence in answer to one who seems to have asked: What kind of creature is it, and what did it indicate? ﴿Tākulu minsaʾatahu﴾ ("it eats his staff"), that is, his staff upon which he died while leaning on it standing up, in a glass house that had no door. The jinn had made it for him when Allah informed him that his term had arrived. A remnant had remained in the mosque in order to conceal his death from the jinn who were working in the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis) until it was completed. Al-Fayruzabadi said in al-Qamus, in the chapter on the hamza: nasaʾahu: he drove it, urged it on, delayed it, and pushed it away from the watering place. Al-minsaʾa, like mikhnasa, is a staff (murtaba, i.e., a fixed form), and the hamza may be dropped in both: it is called al-ʿaṣā ("the staff") because beasts are driven with it, that is, they are urged on. The substitution in it is obligatory, as transmitted by Sibawayh. End of quote. So the meaning is that the jinn were driven and urged on by it. The two Madinans and Abu ʿAmr read it with substitution (ibdāl); Ibn ʿĀmir, through the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan and al-Dajuni from Hisham, read it with the hamza silent; and the rest read it with an open hamza. ﴿Falammā kharra﴾ ("then when he fell"), that is, collapsed to the ground after the termite had gnawed through his staff. ﴿Tabayyanati al-jinnu﴾ ("the jinn became clear"), that is, they knew with clear knowledge, with which they could no longer be capable of embellishment and deception, and their affair was exposed and became fully manifest. ﴿An﴾ ("that") means that they ﴿law kānū﴾ ("if they had been") ﴿yaʿlamūna al-ghayb﴾ ("knowing the unseen"), that is, its knowledge, ﴿mā labithū﴾ ("they would not have remained"), that is, they would not have stayed a year ﴿fī al-ʿadhābi al-muhīn﴾ ("in the humiliating torment"), because of that work in which they were subjugated. The purpose is to nullify what they claimed of knowledge of the unseen in a descriptive manner, because the meaning is that their claim is either a lie or ignorance. The best condition for them is that it be ignorance on their part, and their ignorance has now become clear to them with a clarity they cannot deny. It is also possible that ﴿an﴾ is causal (taʿlīliyya), and the sense would be: the state of the jinn became clear regarding what is supposed about them, that they know the unseen, because they [did not know]... to its end. The cause of their knowledge of his having been dead for the period before that was that they placed the termite on a part of the staff, and it ate from it for a day and a night, and they calculated on that basis and found the period to be a year. In this there is a rebuke to the Arabs, who believe those who prove by this matter that the jinn do not know the unseen, in the superstitions that the soothsayers and others bring them, which deceive them, while they witness from it great falsehood. Thus they were equal to someone among the sons of Adam who reports some of the unseen through a conjecture he holds, or a dream he sees, or something else, so that it happens as he said. This is along with their turning away from one who informs them of the Hereafter out of compassion for them and sincere advice to them, and he never informed them of anything except that its truth became manifest, both before his claim to prophethood and after it, and he showed them of the miracles what dazzled the minds. It has been established that every marvel that was proven for prophets before our Prophet ﷺ, there was proven for him its like or something greater, either for himself or for one of his community. What was mentioned here for Solomon, peace be upon him, of his being preserved for a year after his death, without anything supporting it, has already been proven as its like for a person of this community, without relying on anything. Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri said in his Risala, in the chapter on the Bedouin: "standing [dead]" [mayyitan], not held up by anything. End of quote.

And the like of that person has been established in the lands of Shirwan, in the regions of Fars, near Shamakhi. The name of that saint is Muhammad, and his title is Damdamki.
